blk_part_01_how_a_language_exchange_work.text: A language exchange is a trade: you give something, and you get something back. You help someone with your language, and they help you with theirs. For example, you speak Japanese and want to practise English. So you look for an English speaker who wants to practise Japanese. Everyone is a teacher and a student at the same time.

blk_part_01_how_a_language_exchange_work.text: In this lesson, you visit the Dutch Language Café in The Hague. The Hague is a city in the Netherlands. Every Thursday at 19:30, its language exchange starts. Every visitor gets a language sticker. You write your languages on it and wear it on your shirt. You write the languages you speak, and your native language is one of them. Your native language is the first language you learned as a child. You also write the languages you want to practise. Why a sticker? The room is full of strangers, people you do not know. With one look at a sticker, you know who can help you. A sticker also gives you your first question. Do you see Spanish on someone's sticker? Then ask: I see you study Spanish. Why?

blk_part_01_how_a_language_exchange_work.text: At 20:00, the speed exchange starts. You talk with one person for 3 minutes. Then you move to the next person. You and your partner take turns choosing the language. First one of you chooses, then the other. This way, both people practise. Why only 3 minutes? In a short time, you meet many new people. You also find the people you want to talk to again. At 20:30, everyone sits down at language tables. For example, there is an English table and a Spanish table. At each table, people talk or play games in one language. At 21:10, you can change tables and try a new language.

Koffie verkeerd has a lot of warm milk, often more than the coffee. So it is the wrong way around. It costs €4.00. If you are hungry, try an empanada. An empanada is small and baked, with food inside. Here, you choose cheese, meat or spinach inside. One empanada costs €6.50.

blk_part_04_keeping_the_conversation_goi.text: The best tool for a long conversation is the follow-up question. A follow-up question is a question about what the other person just said. Lucía says: I moved here from Valencia. A new question jumps to a new idea: Do you like football? A follow-up question stays with her idea: Why did you move here? She answers: For work. I work at a hotel. Now you take one part of her answer. Then you ask again: What do you do at the hotel? Each answer gives you the next question.

Follow-up questions worked best. Why? A follow-up question shows that you are really listening. But there is one problem. If you never talk about yourself, people may think you are hiding something. A good conversation goes both ways. React to what you hear, for example: Really? Me too! Or say: That sounds fun! Then tell something about yourself, and ask back.

Teach Daan one useful phrase in your language. Ask at least three follow-up questions. React with Really? Me too! or That sounds fun! At the end, ask for WhatsApp and say: See you next Thursday! Then change roles.
